hook_text: Why does dividing make the number bigger?
clip_script:
Let us pour. You have three litres of juice and cups that hold a quarter of a litre each. How many cups can you fill? That is three divided by one quarter, and you can just count: each litre fills four cups, so three litres fill twelve. Three divided by a quarter is twelve. Dividing by a quarter gave a bigger number than three, because quarter-litre cups are small and lots of them fit.

Now bigger cups: two thirds of a litre each, and you have four litres. How many cups? Each litre is three thirds, so four litres is twelve thirds. Each cup takes two thirds, so twelve thirds fill six cups. Four divided by two thirds is six. And now look at what you actually did with the numbers: four times three to get thirds, then divided by two to make pairs. Four times three over two. That is four times the flipped fraction.
visual_style: Juice jug pouring into a row of cups that fill one by one; fraction flipping with a snap
pacing: steady, a beat as each cup fills
call_to_action: Open the full session to understand flip and multiply, not just obey it.
